statement: In two online surveys of US adults who used kratom (Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian plant; use self-reported and products not tested), both spread mainly through the American Kratom Association, a group that favours kratom use and campaigns to keep it legal, and through other websites frequented by people who use kratom and social media, so that each share describes those respondents only, people most often said they used kratom for pain and for anxiety or depression; many said they had used it to cut down or stop opioids; large majorities ticked benefits such as less pain, more energy and better mood; and smaller numbers reported side effects, feeling unwell when they went without kratom, having needed treatment because of it, or the symptoms of a kratom use disorder. In October 2016 a survey addressed to people currently using kratom was announced on the Association's homepage, Facebook page, forums and members' email list, with weekly reminders, and on other websites frequented by people who use kratom; collection stopped at 10,000 responses and the 8,049 completed ones (80.5%) were analysed (Grundmann, 2017; no specific funding and no conflict declared; the Association did not fund the survey but, the acknowledgment says, distributed it and helped collect responses). Respondents were mostly non-Hispanic White (89.39%); 56.91% were men and 55.09% were aged 31 to 50. Asked yes or no about four reasons, 4,811 of 7,060 (68%) said a medical condition with acute or chronic pain, 4,684 of 7,047 (66.5%) an emotional or mental condition such as anxiety, depression or PTSD, 1,813 of 6,981 (26.0%) a dependency on a prescription medicine such as opioid painkillers, and 539 of 7,029 (7.7%) a dependency on an illicit drug (editors' calculation for the last two). On a checklist of perceived benefits, 6,466 of 7,605 (85.0%) ticked decreased pain, 6,394 of 7,635 (83.75%) increased energy, 6,084 of 7,605 (80.00%) less depressive mood and 3,715 of 7,605 (48.8%, editors' calculation) reduced or stopped use of opioid painkillers. 1,652 of 7,893 (20.93%) reported negative effects, mostly nausea (12.75%), constipation (9.17%) and dizziness or drowsiness (4.81%). 703 respondents, 42.55% of the 1,652 who reported any negative effect (whether the others were asked is not stated), said they had negative effects when they had not taken kratom for more than 12 (240), 24 (304) or 48 hours (159); on a scale from 1 (very severe) to 5 (not severe at all), 67 chose 1, 284 chose 2, 254 chose 3, 81 chose 4 and 17 chose 5, so about half (351, editors' calculation) chose one of the two most severe ratings. Asked whether they had ever needed medical or mental health care because of kratom, 51 of 7,893 (0.65%) said yes (30 for medical and 21 for mental health problems); the Highlights call this the incidence of kratom-related toxicity requiring treatment, but it is a lifetime self-report by people still using kratom, from which people who stopped after harm, and anyone who died, are missing. The abstract concludes that kratom has a dose-dependent opioid-like effect giving perceived relief of pain and mood disorders, but the Results found no dose-dependent effect for decreased pain: the odds of reporting it showed no clear difference by self-reported amount per dose or by doses per week (every interval included no difference). From January to December 2017 a survey of adults who had used kratom in the past year was advertised on sites of interest to people who use kratom (the Association, Erowid and Reddit are given as examples): of 4,302 who began, 2,826 (66%) met the criteria and completed it and 28 were removed, leaving 2,798, of whom 53% had heard of it through the Association and 44.2% through Facebook or other social media (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2020; funded in part by US National Institute on Drug Abuse grants to two authors; no conflicts declared). Their mean age was 40.2; 60.7% were women and 89.8% White; 59.1% used kratom daily and 80.7% had used it in the 24 hours before; 1,924 (68.8%) reported chronic pain in the past 3 months, and 52.9% had ever had opioid withdrawal symptoms or difficulty controlling opioid use. They said they used kratom for pain (2,554, 91.3%), anxiety (1,881, 67.2%) and depression (1,804, 64.5%), and rated it as effective, on average, at 83.3, 76.7 and 76.5 out of 100. On 0-to-100 scales of its typical effects they rated 'good effects' 86.4 and 'drug liking' 85.7, 'alert' 49.8 and 'stimulated' 41.3, 'desire' 30.1, 'euphoric' 25.1 and 'high' 12.0. 1,144 (40.9%) said they had used kratom to help them cut down or stop using heroin or prescription pain medicines; of these, 999 said it had treated their opioid withdrawal symptoms effectively and 911 that it reduced their craving, and 849 reported 6 months or more without opioids that they attributed to kratom; nothing was verified, and prescribed and illicit use of opioid medicines could not be told apart. 540 (19.3%) reported adverse effects of kratom and 357 (12.8%) possible ones; of these 897, 9 rated them serious to extreme and 772 said they lasted a day or less, and 17 (0.6% of all 2,798) sought medical treatment. 267 (9.5%) reported kratom-related withdrawal symptoms and 491 (17.5%) possible ones. On a DSM-5 symptom checklist for the past year, completed by the respondents themselves, 276 (9.9%) met the criteria for mild, 51 (1.8%) for moderate and 17 (0.6%) for severe kratom use disorder: 68 (2.4%) moderate or severe, as Table 2 gives it. The abstract's 56 (2%) matches no figure in that table, whose four rows add up to all 2,798 respondents and agree with the Results' statement that fewer than 3% met these criteria; and the abstract's 411 respondents with more than a year of continuous abstinence from opioids attributed to kratom match no result either: in the Results, 411 is the number of the 1,144 who reported no opioid use in the past year, with nothing on continuity or attribution, while Table 1 implies 594 (editors' calculation). Both surveys rest on what self-selected respondents said; neither tested what people took or checked what they reported, and the 2017 authors say people with negative experiences who stopped using kratom may be under-represented, so that adverse effects may be underestimated and benefits overestimated. Neither compared people who use kratom with people who do not, so neither can show that kratom relieves pain or mood symptoms or helps people stop opioids, or how common any benefit or harm is among people who use kratom. The two teams worked independently but reached people mainly through the same advocacy group a year apart, so their agreement shows that people reached this way answer alike, not that the profile holds for others. Neither survey asked why some people feel little from an amount; in the 2016 survey, respondents reporting the largest amounts per dose reported nausea, vomiting, constipation and dizziness or drowsiness more often than those in each smaller category, in cross-sectional comparisons. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In two online surveys of people in the US who used kratom, found mainly through a group that campaigns to keep kratom legal (8,049 people in 2016 and 2,798 in 2017), pain was the most common reason given (68 and 91 in 100), followed by anxiety or depression (about 2 in 3). Large majorities said kratom eased pain, gave energy or lifted mood; in 2017 people rated its 'good effects' 86 out of 100 but feeling 'high' only 12. In 2017, 1,144 people said they had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids, and 849 said they then went 6 months or more without opioids, which they credited to kratom; none of this was checked. In 2016, 703 said they felt unwell when they went 12 to 48 hours without kratom, about half of them at the severe end of the scale, and 51 of 7,893 had ever needed treatment because of it. In 2017, 68 of 2,798 met a checklist's criteria for moderate or severe kratom use disorder. Both surveys relied on what volunteers said, people who had stopped after bad experiences were left out in 2016 and may have been too few in 2017, and neither compared people who do not use kratom, so they cannot show what kratom does or how common these experiences are.
population: US adults who used kratom, in two self-selected online samples reached mainly through the American Kratom Association, an advocacy group, and through other websites frequented by people who use kratom and social media: 8,049 completed responses (of 10,000 collected) to a survey addressed to people currently using kratom, 2 to 26 October 2016 (56.91% men; 55.09% aged 31 to 50; 89.39% non-Hispanic White); and 2,798 adults who had used kratom in the past year, January to December 2017 (of 4,302 who began; 53% heard of it through the Association; mean age 40.2; 60.7% women; 89.8% White; 59.1% daily use; 68.8% with chronic pain in the past 3 months)
exposure: Kratom used by people's own choice, self-reported and not tested: current use in 2016 (most for 1 to 5 years) or past-year use in 2017 (80.7% in the past 24 hours), almost always swallowed (powder, tea or capsules); amounts per dose not given here
comparator: None: neither survey included people who do not use kratom; within the 2016 survey, respondents reporting smaller amounts per dose or fewer doses per week are compared with the largest categories, and within the 2017 survey, respondents who had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids (1,144) with the others (1,654)
outcome: Self-reported reasons for use, perceived benefits and effectiveness ratings, typical effects, use to cut down or stop opioids and opioid abstinence attributed to kratom, negative and adverse effects, effects of going without kratom and withdrawal symptoms, lifetime need for treatment because of kratom (2016), and a self-completed DSM-5 checklist for past-year kratom use disorder (2017)
magnitude: Grundmann (2017), 8,049 respondents (denominators vary by item): reasons, pain 4,811/7,060 (68%), emotional or mental condition 4,684/7,047 (66.5%), prescription-medicine dependency 1,813/6,981 (26.0%, editors' calculation), illicit-drug dependency 539/7,029 (7.7%, editors' calculation); perceived benefits, decreased pain 6,466/7,605 (85.0%), increased energy 6,394/7,635 (83.75%), less depressive mood 6,084/7,605 (80.00%), less anxious mood 5,978/7,605, elevated mood 5,790/7,605, increased focus 5,299/7,605, reduced or stopped opioid painkillers 3,715/7,605 (48.8%, editors' calculation), reduced PTSD symptoms 1,300/7,605; any negative effect 1,652/7,893 (20.93%): nausea 12.75% (970), constipation 9.17% (697), dizziness or drowsiness 4.81% (366); negative effects when kratom was not taken, 703 of the 1,652 (42.55%; 240 after more than 12 hours, 304 after 24, 159 after 48; at least 8.9% of 7,893, editors' calculation), rated 1 (very severe) by 67 (9.53%), 2 by 284 (40.40%), 3 by 254 (36.13%), 4 by 81 (11.52%), 5 (not severe at all) by 17 (2.42%); ever needed medical or mental health care because of kratom 51/7,893 (0.65%; 30 medical, 21 mental health; Wilson 95% interval 0.49% to 0.85%, editors' calculation, chance only); decreased pain against the largest amount-per-dose category, odds ratios 1.12 to 1.25, and against the most frequent dosing category, 0.65 to 1.62, every interval including 1; nausea in smaller amount categories against the largest, odds ratios 0.23 (0.15 to 0.35) to 0.58 (0.43 to 0.77). Garcia-Romeu et al. (2020), 2,798 respondents: reasons, pain 2,554 (91.3%), anxiety 1,881 (67.2%), depression 1,804 (64.5%), post-traumatic stress 829 (29.6%), bipolar mood 687 (24.6%), cutting down or stopping opioids 1,144 (40.9%); mean effectiveness (0 to 100) pain 83.3 (SD 18.5), anxiety 76.7 (24.3), depression 76.5 (25.4); typical effects (0 to 100) good effects 86.4, drug liking 85.7, alert 49.8, stimulated 41.3, desire 30.1, euphoric 25.1, high 12.0; of the 1,144, withdrawal treated effectively 999 (87.3%), craving reduced 911 (79.6%), 6 months or more without opioids attributed to kratom 849 (74.2%), no past-year opioid use 411 (35.9%; Table 1 implies 594, editors' calculation); adverse effects yes 540 (19.3%), maybe 357 (12.8%); of these 897, serious to extreme 9, lasting a day or less 772; sought medical treatment 17 (0.6%); withdrawal symptoms yes 267 (9.5%), maybe 491 (17.5%), mean Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale score 8.8 (SD 8.4) among those who completed it, in the authors' mild range; DSM-5 checklist, past year, none 2,454 (87.7%), mild 276 (9.9%), moderate 51 (1.8%), severe 17 (0.6%), moderate or severe 68 (2.4%; Wilson 95% interval 1.9% to 3.1%, editors' calculation, chance only; the abstract's 56 (2%) not used); troubled by kratom use 3.2 (SD 9.8) out of 100. No comparison with people who do not use kratom, so no difference can be given.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Methods (PDF p. 3); 2.1 Survey setting, approval, and data collection (one paragraph, PDF p. 6); 3.1 Demographics (one paragraph, PDF p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Anonymous cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics), described in the abstract as conducted in October 2016 among 10,000 people currently using kratom through social media and online resources of the American Kratom Association. It was announced on the Association's homepage and social media outlets (Facebook page, website forums and membership email distribution) with weekly reminders until 10,000 responses were reached, and shared on other websites frequented by people who use kratom, two of which are named (speciosa.org, drugs-forum.com); no incentive; respondents had to acknowledge being 18 or older; data were collected from 2 to 26 October 2016 and only the 8,049 completed responses (80.5%) were analysed; IP addresses were used, without being stored, to block repeat responses from one device. The author states that the recruitment method likely introduced selection bias, because electronic distribution may skew toward a younger and economically better-off population with internet access, under-representing people with low incomes and those without online skills or internet access. Respondents: 56.91% men, 55.09% aged 31 to 50, 54.25% married or partnered, 89.39% non-Hispanic White, 56.83% employed for wages, 61.31% privately insured, 63.24% with household income of $35,000 or more, 82.32% with at least some college.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (PDF p. 3); 3.3 Self-reported beneficial effects of Kratom use (one paragraph, PDF p. 10); Table 4, header row and decreased-pain columns (PDF p. 24)
evidence.extracted: The abstract concludes that kratom shows a dose-dependent opioid-like effect providing self-reported perceived benefits in alleviating pain and relieving mood disorders. Results: the most frequent perceived benefits were decreased pain (85.01%), increased energy (83.75%) and less depressive mood (80.00%); Table 4 header counts: decreased pain 6,466 yes and 1,139 no; increased energy 6,394 and 1,241; less depressive mood 6,084 and 1,521; less anxious mood 5,978 and 1,627; elevated mood 5,790 and 1,815; increased focus 5,299 and 2,306; reduced or stopped the use of opioid painkillers 3,715 and 3,890; reduced PTSD symptoms 1,300 and 6,305. The Results state that no dose-dependent beneficial effect was observed for decreased pain, increased focus or reduced PTSD symptoms: in Table 4 the odds ratios for decreased pain against the largest amount-per-dose category were 1.12 to 1.25 (intervals from 0.77-1.61 to 0.90-1.74) and against the most frequent dosing category 0.65 to 1.62 (intervals from 0.34-1.23 to 0.59-4.44), every interval including 1. Smaller self-reported amounts went with lower odds of some other benefits (increased energy, less depressive and anxious mood, elevated mood, reducing or stopping opioid painkillers). Editors' calculation: 6,466 of 7,605 is 85.0%, and 3,715 of 7,605 is 48.8%.

evidence.extracted: The authors write that the study supports earlier ones in suggesting that kratom has a relatively benign risk profile compared to typical opioids, with only a minority endorsing adverse effects, withdrawal symptoms or problematic use (the survey included no comparison with opioids), and that respondents using kratom daily were unlikely to meet criteria for a kratom-related use disorder (no such analysis is reported). They state that the major limitation is the self-selected convenience sample: because data were collected online and recruitment ran through websites of interest to people who use kratom, the sample likely exhibits selection bias toward people who are younger, more affluent and more positively inclined towards kratom, so that the results may under-represent people of lower socio-economic status, older and less technologically fluent people, and those with negative experiences of kratom (for example, people who stopped because of adverse effects), and adverse effects may be underestimated and benefits overestimated; and that medically prescribed and illicit use of opioid medications could not be distinguished. They call for nationally representative and controlled studies. Funding: support for two authors (Griffiths, Dunn) in part by NIDA grants; no conflicts of interest to report; the authors thank Dr Jack E. Henningfield for comments on early drafts.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement (cards sc_grundmann_2017 and sc_garcia_romeu_2020: JBI prevalence checklist, editors' summary high for both): everything is self-reported online, without testing of the product or of use and without verification of opioid abstinence; the 2016 checklists of reasons, benefits, negative effects and effects of going without kratom are unvalidated, the going-without item counts answers only among the 1,652 who reported a negative effect, item denominators vary from 6,981 to 7,893 without explanation, and the treatment item is lifetime and does not separate outpatient care from hospital; the 2017 survey used standard instruments (DSM-5 checklist, Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale), self-completed online. Both papers print headline figures that their Results do not support (2016: dose-dependent pain relief, and 0.65% called an incidence; 2017: 56 with moderate or severe use disorder against Table 2's 68, and 411 with more than a year of continuous abstinence attributed to kratom), which the claim corrects from the Results and tables.

inconsistency.note: The two surveys agree on the main reasons (pain, then anxiety or depression), on high perceived benefit and on few respondents reporting treatment; their shares differ (pain 68 against 91 in 100) as their questions and samples differ, so they are given side by side, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Coverage: both samples are self-selected volunteers reached mainly through one advocacy organization that favours kratom use and campaigns for its legality (in 2016 the survey was announced on its channels and the organization helped collect responses; in 2017, 53% heard of the survey through it), plus other websites frequented by people who use kratom and social media; people who stopped using kratom, including after harm, are absent (2016: addressed to people currently using kratom, by their own declaration) or may be under-represented (2017, as its authors say), and anyone who died is absent; respondents were mostly White, employed, middle-aged and in the US, surveyed in 2016 and 2017. The shares describe these respondents, not people who use kratom generally.

imprecision.note: Large samples (8,049 and 2,798); the rare counts (51, 17, 68) are given as counts, with chance-only intervals in the magnitude, and no comparison rests on them.

dose_response.note: The 2016 associations between the largest self-reported amounts per dose and more negative effects are cross-sectional comparisons against one category, with self-reported amounts; not a basis for rating up, and the claim is descriptive.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the people sampled (METHODS 6.3): starts low; down one for risk of bias (measurement) and one for indirectness (coverage): very low, the floor, which either downgrade alone would reach; never upgraded. Status replicated: two independent teams (University of Florida, 2016; Johns Hopkins and the NIDA Intramural Research Program, 2017), with different questionnaires, agree on the kinds of reasons given and on how few reported needing treatment; both recruited mainly through the same advocacy organization a year apart, so respondents may overlap and the agreement shows that people reached this way answer alike, not that the profile holds for people who use kratom generally; it does not raise the certainty. The claim reports what respondents said about kratom's effects and about using it to cut down or stop opioids; it does not say that kratom relieves pain or mood symptoms or helps anyone stop opioids, which neither survey could show, and it gives no advice on using kratom for opioid use or withdrawal. Corrections from the Results and tables: the 2017 abstract's 56 (2%) with moderate or severe use disorder is replaced by Table 2's 68 (2.4%), because Table 2's four rows add up to all 2,798 respondents and agree with the Results' statement that fewer than 3% met the criteria, while 56 matches no row or sum; the abstract's 411 with more than a year of continuous abstinence attributed to kratom is not used, because the Results give 411 as the number with no opioid use in the past year, without continuity or attribution (and Table 1 implies 594); the 2016 Highlights' incidence of 0.65% is described as what was asked, a lifetime self-report by people still using kratom; and the 2016 abstract's dose-dependent pain relief is set against the Results, which found none for decreased pain. Amounts per dose are not given, so that nothing reads as guidance on amounts. Funding and conflicts as printed: 2016, no specific grant and no conflict, the organization having distributed the survey and helped collect responses without funding it; 2017, NIDA grants to two authors and no conflicts.

statement: In overdose deaths entered into the CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS) from 27 US states between July 2016 and December 2017 (11 states for the whole period and 16 more for July to December 2017 only; five states sent county subsets covering at least 75% of their overdose deaths), a system that takes unintentional and undetermined-intent overdose deaths in which at least one opioid contributed, plus overdose deaths to which kratom contributed, kratom (Mitragyna speciosa, a Southeast Asian plant) was detected on postmortem toxicology in 152 of 27,338 deaths (0.56%, about 6 in 1,000) (Olsen et al., 2019; a CDC report by CDC staff; no potential conflicts disclosed). A medical examiner or coroner named kratom as a cause of death in 91 of the 152; for 7 of the 91, kratom was the only substance that tested positive, though the report adds that other substances cannot be ruled out for them, so at least one other substance tested positive in 84 of the 91 (editors' calculation). Other substances listed as a cause of death, among the 152 and the 91: any fentanyl, including analogues, 99 (65.1%) and 51 (56.0%); heroin 50 (32.9%) and 23 (25.3%); benzodiazepines 34 (22.4%) and 24 (26.4%); prescription opioids (a coded class of substances, with drugs prescribed to the person who died not told apart from diverted ones) 30 (19.7%) and 22 (24.2%); cocaine 28 (18.4%) and 15 (16.5%); alcohol 19 (12.5%) and 11 (12.1%); methamphetamine 13 (8.6%) among the 152 (not shown for the 91). These counts are of substances named as a cause, not of all substances detected, and several could be named for one death; the report's statement that postmortem testing found several substances in almost all decedents points to this table, which does not show it for the 152. Death-investigation records showed a history of substance misuse for 123 of the 152 (80.9%) and 71 of the 91 (78.0%), and no evidence of current medically supervised pain treatment for 138 (90.8%) and 80 (87.9%); ages are not reported. The report says that postmortem testing protocols were not documented and varied among and within states, and that identifying kratom depends on the method, so these data might underestimate kratom-positive deaths to an extent that cannot be determined; it does not say how many of the deaths were tested for kratom, nor the criteria for naming it as a cause. Because the system takes only deaths in which an opioid or kratom contributed, 0.56% is not kratom's share of all overdose deaths; with no count of people who use kratom there is no death rate; and the counts cannot show how much kratom contributed beside the other drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a CDC count of 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states between July 2016 and December 2017 (deaths in which an opioid or kratom played a part), kratom was found in 152, about 6 in every 1,000. Death investigators named kratom as a cause in 91 of these; in 84 of the 91 at least one other drug was found too, and fentanyl was named as a cause in 51. Only 7 had kratom as the only drug found, and the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out even for them. About 8 in 10 of the people who died had a recorded history of substance misuse. How kratom was tested for varied between and within states and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed; the report cannot show how much kratom contributed beside the other drugs, kratom's share of all overdose deaths, or a death rate among people who use kratom.
population: 27,338 unintentional or undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths entered into the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS) from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017 (11 states for the whole period, 16 for July to December 2017 only; five states with county subsets covering at least 75% of their overdose deaths): deaths in which at least one opioid contributed, plus overdose deaths to which kratom contributed; data as of 22 January 2019
exposure: Kratom detected on postmortem toxicology (kratom-positive, 152), and kratom named as a cause of death by a medical examiner or coroner (kratom-involved, 91, all among the 152); testing protocols not documented and varying among and within states; specimen, method, concentrations and criteria for naming a cause not reported
comparator: None: no comparison with SUDORS deaths without kratom; the two groups described overlap (the 91 are among the 152)
outcome: Share of SUDORS overdose deaths with kratom detected; kratom named as a cause; kratom as the only substance detected; other substances named as causes; recorded circumstances (history of substance misuse, supervised pain treatment, previous overdose)
magnitude: Olsen et al. (2019): kratom detected in 152 of 27,338 SUDORS overdose deaths (0.56%; about 6 in 1,000, editors' calculation); named as a cause in 91 of the 152 (59.9%); kratom the only substance testing positive in 7 of the 91, so at least one other substance in 84 (92.3%, editors' calculation); kratom detected but not named as a cause in 61 (editors' calculation). Substances listed as a cause, kratom-positive (152) and kratom-involved (91): any fentanyl 99 (65.1%) and 51 (56.0%); heroin 50 (32.9%) and 23 (25.3%); benzodiazepines 34 (22.4%) and 24 (26.4%); prescription opioids (a coded class; prescribed and diverted drugs not distinguished) 30 (19.7%) and 22 (24.2%); cocaine 28 (18.4%) and 15 (16.5%); alcohol 19 (12.5%) and 11 (12.1%); methamphetamine 13 (8.6%) and not shown. History of substance misuse 123 (80.9%) and 71 (78.0%); no evidence of supervised pain treatment 138 (90.8%) and 80 (87.9%); previous overdose 13 and 10 (11.0%); men 116 (76.3%) and 69 (75.8%). No comparison group, no death rate.

evidence.locator: Text, 2nd paragraph (left column, continued at the top of the right column); footnotes †, § and ¶
evidence.extracted: CDC funds 32 states and the District of Columbia to abstract into SUDORS detailed data on unintentional and undetermined-intent opioid overdose deaths from death certificates and medical examiner and coroner reports, including postmortem toxicology; overdose deaths involving kratom, including nonopioid overdose deaths, are included (footnote §: fatal overdoses in which at least one opioid contributed, plus those with no contributing opioid if a substance with opioid-like properties contributed, kratom currently being the only such substance). SUDORS records all substances testing positive on postmortem toxicology, whether or not they contributed, although testing varies in scope among medical examiners and coroners. The analysis covers 11 states for July 2016 to June 2017 and 27 states for July to December 2017 (footnote ¶ names them); Florida, Illinois, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Washington submit data for county subsets reflecting at least 75% of their overdose deaths (footnote †); data current as of January 22, 2019.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement (card sc_olsen_2019: JBI prevalence checklist, editors' summary high): whether, how and in which specimen kratom was tested for was not documented and varied among and within states, and identification is method-dependent, so the count of kratom-positive deaths is a floor of unknown size, as the authors say; the share of the 27,338 deaths tested for kratom and the criteria by which medical examiners and coroners named kratom as a cause are not reported; the table lists substances named as causes, not all substances detected.

indirectness.note: Worded for what was counted: deaths entered into SUDORS from 27 states (unequal periods; county subsets in five states), which takes overdose deaths in which an opioid or kratom contributed, in July 2016 to December 2017; not worded as kratom's share of all overdose deaths, a rate among people who use kratom, or a figure for later years, other products or other countries.

imprecision.note: 152 and 91 deaths; the 7 deaths with kratom as the only substance detected are given as a count, and nothing rests on a precise estimate of them.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a surveillance count.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS 6.3): a count from death records starts low; down one for risk of bias (undocumented, varying toxicology testing and unstated criteria for naming kratom as a cause): very low; never upgraded. Status single study. 'Kratom-involved' is described as what it is, a certifier's listing of kratom as a cause, almost always beside other substances, not a death caused by kratom alone; the 84 of 91 with at least one other substance testing positive is editors' arithmetic from the report's 7 with kratom alone, and the report itself cautions that other substances cannot be ruled out even in those 7. The report's statement that testing found several substances in almost all decedents is given as its statement, because the table it cites lists only substances named as causes. The printed 8.5% for 13 of 152 deaths with a previous overdose (8.6% in the methamphetamine row) is a rounding slip and is not used. The report gives no ages, specimens or concentrations, and its kratom-positive count is described by its authors as a possible underestimate. A CDC report by CDC staff, from a CDC-funded system; no potential conflicts disclosed.
